  3. then the next best.

applications an employer would take seriously, not on throughput.

## How to file one

1. Open the DIRECT application link, never the aggregator (`go.landed.jobs/...` and the like
   are redirect trackers — follow them to the real ATS page, then work there). Greenhouse,
   Lever, Ashby and Workday are the common ones.
2. browser_snapshot the form. Read every field and its label before typing anything.
3. Fill from facts.md and resume.txt, field by field:
   - Identity, contact, links — straight from facts.md.

     text, paste the letter's body, not its markdown headers. If it wants a file and only the
     markdown exists, say so in the output and treat the application as blocked.
   - Free-text screener questions ("why us", "describe a project") — write them from real
     evidence in resume.txt and the draft. Never invent a project, employer, date, or number.
   - Demographic / EEO questions — the facts.md answer, which is "decline to self-identify"

   resume.txt, you do not answer it. You stop that application, record the exact question in

   work-authorization, salary, education, or background-check question is a lie on a legal

5. Re-read the filled form with browser_snapshot and browser_screenshot before sending. Check

# Cover letter — MATS Residency, Winter 2027

Tailored to: https://www.matsprogram.org/residency/apply · https://www.matsprogram.org/program/winter-2027
Date drafted: 2026-08-31
Deadline: October 31, 2026 (11:59pm AoE)

> NOTE: This is a draft only — not submitted. The MATS Residency Winter 2027 is in-person
> (Berkeley, CA and/or London, UK) over 12 weeks, January 19–April 10, 2027. The applicant is
> US-based; the logistics of a 12-week physical presence are the applicant's to resolve.

Dear MATS Residency Selection Committee,

I am applying to the Winter 2027 MATS Residency because I want to do real research on making
advanced AI safe, and I have spent the last few years building AI systems end-to-end — the
hands-on ability to run experiments, implement models, and debug my own code — and the honest
curiosity about where the technology goes that I now want to point toward safety.

My ML work is practical and complete, from idea to deployment. At Hewani I architected and
deployed an end-to-end recommendation system on Google Cloud Vertex AI, owning the full
lifecycle from infrastructure provisioning through containerization to monitoring and
retraining. At Mutual of Omaha I built a retrieval-augmented-generation system over insurance
document corpora and an agentic small-language-model ETL pipeline that deduplicates medical
and insurance claims. These are not API wrappers — they are systems where I had to design
the model, the data, and the evaluation, and then make them reliable in production.

More relevantly for MATS, I have been building at the frontier edge of a field that is
itself raising alignment-adjacent questions. My hybrid quantum-classical ML project compares
QSVC and VQC models against classical baselines on a biomedical knowledge graph, choosing
models on measured PR-AUC rather than assumption — the discipline of an evaluator, not just a
builder. I have run quantum circuits against real IBM hardware via Qiskit and PennyLane, and I
built a post-quantum random-number generator validated against the NIST test suites. That
combination — implementing models, running them, and rigorously checking whether they actually
do what I claimed — is exactly the "strong ML background; run experiments, implement papers,
debug your own code" bar you describe.

I know I am not a traditional candidate: there is no PhD, no formal "researcher" title, no
publication list behind me. That is deliberate. I am a self-taught engineer — an ADI
Applied-Data Fellow and, before that, a full-stack Java academy graduate — who has learned to
ship AI for real, and I want to apply that to the questions I find most urgent. I have
already spent time thinking about where AI is going, through hackathons, an AI-Society
membership, and projects where I deliberately chose the path with the harder-to-justify
metrics. I take initiative, I work autonomously, and I can show progress at the end of a week.

The MATS Residency is where I would rather learn than watch. Give me the problem and I will
get to work at industry speed — and I will bring the habits of someone who has had to make AI
systems trustworthy in production, not just in a notebook.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Jonathan Beale
jonaston015@gmail.com · linkedin.com/in/jonathan-beale · github.com/iconbaypark2900

This is a strategic editing plan, not a rewritten resume. Do not invent experience or dates.

Three intake windows. Rolling start dates.

Applications are reviewed by the MATS Residency team with input from the program's advisors where appropriate. You will hear about the outcome of your application by the end of November 2026. Shortlisted applicants will then be invited to an interview or a paid work test in the first week of December 2026, depending on track and research area. Information about the interview and the panel members will be shared beforehand. Selected Residents will be informed by the end of 2026, with a plan to start in early 2027.

Application window

Aug 25 to Oct 31, 2026

The 2027 Winter intake window opens on 25 August 2026 and closes on 31 October 2026 (AoE, Anywhere on Earth). You can apply now here.

The next application window after this one opens in March 2027. The Residency is open to applicants internationally, and MATS provides visa support for those relocating from abroad.

Who should apply

We assess the quality and seriousness of your work, not the titles or credentials on your CV. You do not need a PhD, a role with "researcher" in your title, an extensive publication record, or a prior background in AI safety to be a strong applicant. The Residency is looking for talented individuals capable of producing outstanding AI safety research, including many whose best work is confidential, unpublished, or outside traditional research roles. If you are unsure whether you fit, we encourage you to apply or email us first.

What research is the Residency looking to fund?

As part of your application, we ask you to submit a brief plan for the work you want to do during the Residency: a research plan, a plan for the safety-relevant work you want to build or test, or a business plan for Incubation. When we assess fit, we look for:

Impact first: ambitious, longer-term work that does not sit neatly in academia or industry, judged above all by how much it could reduce catastrophic risk from AI.
Depth: foundational questions that take years, not weeks, to pay off.

The areas we are most excited about right now are:

Safe automation of alignment research: keeping AI-assisted research checkable and maintaining meaningful oversight as AI capabilities grow beyond human review.
Safety cases, evaluations, AI strategy, AI assurance, and technical AI governance: building the evidence base and frameworks for informed decisions and verifiable policies about advanced AI.
Agentic and multi-agent AI safety and alignment: safety and alignment for AI systems that act autonomously and interact with other agents.

We share these areas to be transparent about the directions we are especially interested in supporting, not to limit your independent research. Propose the work you believe matters most for AI alignment and reducing catastrophic risk from AI, and explain its theory of change. We are excited to see what you come up with.

Choosing your preferred office

Applicants indicate a preference for London, Berkeley, or Washington, DC in their application. Choose the location that provides the greatest proximity to the labs, collaborators, and research community most relevant to your work. The Residency is hybrid, and Residents are expected to spend at least a third of their Residency working in person from these offices. There is no formal base office assignment: Residents can spend their in-person time at any of the offices and move between offices during the program. If more than one office would work equally well for your research, please indicate this on your application.

Application Requirements

All applicants submit the following materials through the online application:

A short profile and eligibility section: Your contact details, current affiliation, CV (maximum 2 pages), office preference, availability for the intake, work-authorization status, highest degree, and any previous MATS involvement. This takes a few minutes, is mostly for routing and logistics, and is not itself assessed.
Track choice: Your chosen track, and a two-to-three-sentence note on why it fits. Reviewers use this note to spot early on whether a different track might suit you better.
References: Submit two references who can speak directly to the quality of your work. If your strongest work is confidential or was completed as part of a larger team, your referees may attest to your contribution in place of publicly available evidence. Some tracks have additional requirements for referees. See the track-specific requirements below.
Representative work sample: Submit one work sample that best represents your strongest or most relevant work. This might include a paper, repository, technical report, evaluation, policy analysis, or another substantial research output.
Written responses: Complete two short written responses and a brief counterfactual question about what you would do if you were not offered a place in the Residency.

Research plan: Submit a brief research plan describing the work you intend to pursue during the Residency and its theory of change.
Why Bridge? Write a short statement explaining why the Residency is the right opportunity for you now.
